_comment: Scalars an author can type into a spreadsheet cell, and the YAML
each one has to be written as. Shared with the Telar Compositor,
which serialises the same fields on its own publish path and keeps
its own copy: one corpus, two implementations, in the manner of
tests/fixtures/column-headers.json.
Both sides maintain the union, so a scalar either side has been
caught by is a scalar both are tested against. Three of these came
from the Compositor and are the ones a list written from scratch
misses: sexagesimals and dates, alternate number bases, and the
float specials.
`expected_yaml` binds the framework serialiser only: it is the exact
bytes PyYAML writes for the scalar here, and a change in them fails
this repository's test. The Compositor's serialiser quotes
differently and pins only the property above, value and type, so a
green run there is agreement on meaning, never on bytes.
`intended_type` is what the author meant the cell to be. It is
'string' throughout, because a cell is text: the property that
matters is that `yes`, `1234` and `12:30` come back as the text
they were typed as rather than as a boolean, an integer and a
sexagesimal. `expected_yaml` is the scalar as this side writes it,
quoting included, so a change of quoting style is visible in a
diff rather than only in a passing test.
Two of the Compositor's cases are excluded here: a value with a bare
carriage return and one with a CRLF pair. The Compositor's serialiser
normalises both to a single LF on its publish path, for a documented
reason; the framework writes back what the author typed, CR and CRLF
included. The two sides have different correct values for the same
source, so the union cannot hold one entry that both agree on — those
two stay Compositor-only.
